questions.q: What makes data skew different from a general large-data-volume problem?
options: Skew only happens on objects with fewer than 1,000 records
Skew is a concentration problem — a disproportionate share of records under one owner, parent, or lookup target — that can occur regardless of the object's overall size
Skew only applies to objects without any lookup fields
Skew is a storage-cost problem, not a performance problem
questions.explain: A relatively small object can have serious skew if its records are heavily concentrated under one owner or parent, while a very large, evenly-distributed object can have none — skew is about concentration, not raw size.

questions.q: Which record count does Salesforce's Trailhead guidance commonly cite as the point where skew concentration starts to matter in practice?
options: Roughly 10,000 records under one owner or parent, treated as a planning guideline rather than a hard platform limit
100 records
1 million records, enforced as a strict system limit
There is no commonly cited figure at all
questions.explain: Trailhead's guidance cites roughly 10,000 child records under one parent (or owned by one user) as the commonly used threshold where skew-related problems tend to start, while being clear it's a guideline, not an enforced platform ceiling.

questions.q: Why are Account and Opportunity specifically called out for parent (account) skew, more so than an arbitrary custom object?
options: Because they are the only two objects that support lookup fields
Because Account and Opportunity records are stored in skinny tables by default
Because their private sharing model requires briefly locking the parent record for certain operations on child records, which creates lock contention when too many children sit under one parent
Because they are the only objects affected by selectivity thresholds
questions.explain: Account and Opportunity have special parent-child sharing behavior under certain sharing models that requires locking the parent during certain child-record operations — a mechanism that creates the specific lock-contention risk covered in the next lesson when too many children accumulate under one parent.

questions.q: A custom "Status Reference" object has a single record that 4 million rows across another object all point to via an ordinary lookup field. What type of skew is this?
options: Ownership skew
Parent (account) skew
This isn't a form of skew because no sharing model is involved
Lookup skew
questions.explain: Lookup skew happens when a very large number of records reference the same target record through an ordinary lookup field, on any object — it doesn't require the Account/Opportunity-specific sharing-lock mechanism that defines parent skew.

questions.q: What SOQL-based technique does this lesson recommend for detecting skew proactively, before it causes a production incident?
options: Disabling all triggers on the object and seeing if performance improves
Running an aggregate SOQL query that groups child records by their parent lookup field (or by OwnerId for ownership skew) and sorts by count, to surface concentration directly
Waiting for a Salesforce Support case to flag the problem automatically
Converting the object to a Big Object, which eliminates skew by design
questions.explain: Grouping records by parent lookup or by OwnerId and sorting by count surfaces parent skew or ownership skew directly, with particular attention to integration users and queue owners as common unintentional sources.
